formats.name: Pattern Interrupt
formats.definition: An opening frame, sound or action that breaks the viewer's scroll expectation (a mid-action start, sudden movement toward the lens, a splash, an extreme close-up, an impossible visual) so the thumb stops before the viewer consciously decides.
formats.when: Reaching cold (non-follower) audiences, and any niche where frame 1 would otherwise look like every other post (a generic gym floor, a generic treatment room). Always pair it with a verbal or text hook within 1–2 s. An interrupt that has nothing to do with the payoff raises swipe-aways.
steps: Start mid-action, with no intro, no logo sting and no 'hey guys'.
Make frame 1 look different from the feed: extreme close-up, low or overhead angle, motion toward the lens, a snap-zoom, water or ice impact.
Within 1–2 s, say or show why it matters (a text hook of 8 words or fewer).
Keep the interrupt on-topic so it doesn't read as bait.
Check Instagram retention (3-second hold) or YouTube 'Viewed vs swiped away' to see whether it worked.

formats.when: The default hook for visual service businesses: the final photo or film frame, the client's face as they exit the plunge, the DEXA result screen, the 'after' posture. It was the strongest single hook type in OpusClip's 2026 dataset.
steps: Open on the best 1–2 s of the whole piece (the final image, the plunge, the scan number).
Add a text label that frames it ('Shot on iPhone, 2 lights, 0 budget' / 'Her body fat 6 months later').
Cut to 'Here's how' and show the process fast, with a new shot every 1–2 s.
End on the result again so the video loops.

formats.name: Stitch / Duet / Remix Response
formats.definition: Reuse part of another creator's video to react, correct or build on it. On TikTok, Stitch plays a few seconds of their clip before your response and Duet places the videos side by side. Instagram Remix is the equivalent.
formats.when: Use it to ride a viral claim in your niche (a wrong ice-bath protocol, a gym myth, a 'massage cures X' claim) by borrowing its context, and to position yourself as an authority through polite correction. Don't use it on Instagram as a downloaded re-upload, because the originality rules demand a transformative addition.
steps: Find a high-view, high-comment video that makes a claim in your niche.
Stitch only the claim (about 5 s), then answer within 2 s with your credential and verdict.
Add new value such as a demo, data or your own client footage, not just a reaction face.
Keep the tone respectful. Contrarian is not the same as insulting.
On Instagram, use Remix or re-record as a green-screen. Never re-upload another creator's file or a watermarked file.

example.creator: Khaby Lame (@khaby.lame)
example.description: Silent stitch and duet reactions to over-complicated 'life hack' videos, ending with a simple fix and his signature shrug.
example.stats: Widely reported as TikTok's most-followed account from June 2022 (not re-verified this session)

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence and platform design: these are native response tools. Instagram's 2024 and April 2026 originality updates demote unedited reposts and aggregator accounts, but still allow third-party material that is meaningfully enhanced. Low-effort edits don't meet the threshold. No large-sample performance study of stitches was found.

production.transitions: None; the stitch cut is the transition

formats.name: Green-Screen React / Explainer
formats.definition: The creator stands in front of a screenshot, article, study, review or video (using the green-screen effect) and comments on it.
formats.when: Explaining a study or news item (a cold-exposure paper, a DEXA vs BMI article), reacting to a client's result screenshot or a Google review, or debunking a viral claim with visual proof.
steps: Pick one visual proof: a study headline, a DEXA printout (with consent), a review screenshot.
The hook is the most surprising line on screen, highlighted.
Point at what you're discussing and zoom the background as you go.
Make one claim per video and cite the source in the caption or a pinned comment.

example.creator: Hank Green (@hankgreen1)
example.description: Frequent green-screen explainers over news articles and science papers on TikTok.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Commentary over source material counts as transformative under Instagram's originality rules. Instagram's Edits app (launched April 2025) ships green-screen and cutout tools, which shows the platform invests in this workflow.

formats.name: POV (Point-of-View) Scenario
formats.definition: A 'POV:' text overlay drops the viewer into a role ('POV: your therapist finds the knot you didn't know you had'), often shot first-person or with the other character addressing the lens.
formats.when: Relatable, emotional or humorous positioning for experiential services (massage, ice bath, a photo shoot) where you want the viewer to imagine being the client. It is highly sendable ('this is you').
steps: Write the POV line as on-screen text in frame 1 (10 words or fewer).
Shoot from the client's eye line, or have the 'other' character look into the lens.
Use natural sound or a licensed trending sound that fits the mood.
Land a micro-payoff (relief, a laugh, a reveal) by 5–8 s and make it loopable.

example.creator: Genre-wide TikTok/Reels text convention (since 2020)
example.description: 'POV:' is one of the longest-running native short-form text conventions. Character-skit creators such as Kris Collins (@kallmekris) build audiences on scenario skits addressed to the viewer.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Mechanism: relatable scenarios drive DM sends, which Mosseri named as a top-3 ranking signal (Jan 2025) and as weighing more for reach to non-followers.

production.audio: Licensed trending sound or natural sound

formats.name: Negative / Warning Hook ('Stop doing X')
formats.definition: Loss-framed openers: 'Stop doing X', 'Don't book a massage until you know this', 'The mistake ruining your ice bath'.
formats.when: Educational content where the audience is already doing the behaviour. Loss framing beats gain framing on attention. Use it in roughly one post in four at most, because constant fear framing erodes trust and can read as clickbait.
steps: Name the specific mistake in 8 words or fewer, both on screen and spoken.
Show the wrong way first (1–2 s), then the fix.
Give the mechanism (why) in one line.
End with 'do this instead' as the saveable payoff.

example.creator: Jeff Nippard (science-based fitness)
example.description: Technique and training videos often framed around common mistakes and myths, followed by the evidence-based fix.

formats.evidence: Robertson et al., Nature Human Behaviour (2023), analysed about 105k headline A/B tests (Upworthy). Each additional negative word raised click-through rate by roughly 2.3%. That study covers headlines, not video, but it supports negative framing as an attention lever. No platform-specific video study was found.

production.transitions: A hard cut on 'instead'; a red/green or X/check overlay

formats.name: Contrarian Take
formats.definition: Challenge the consensus in your niche ('Ice baths right after lifting may blunt muscle gains', 'Your BMI is lying to you').
formats.when: Building authority when you have real evidence for the contrarian position. It must be defensible, because health misinformation hurts trust and can trigger platform policy issues.
steps: State the common belief, then flip it in sentence 2.
Back it with a visual source (a study screenshot, a DEXA readout).
Add nuance at the end ('when it's fine') so you invite debate without being wrong.
Pin a comment with the citation.

example.creator: Andrew Huberman (Huberman Lab)
example.description: Popularised the advice to avoid cold-water immersion right after strength training when the goal is hypertrophy. This is based on Roberts et al. 2015 (J Physiol), which found that post-exercise cold-water immersion attenuated long-term strength-training adaptations.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. OpusClip 2026 lists 'Expert Explainer' among the most common viral storylines. Contrarian hooks drive comments, but Mosseri's named top signals are watch time, likes per reach and sends per reach, so the take still has to hold attention. The underlying science example is Roberts LA et al., J Physiol 2015.

production.transitions: Green-screen or B-roll cutaways for the evidence

formats.name: Curiosity Gap / Open Loop
formats.definition: Open a specific question or tease a payoff that only resolves later ('Wait for her scan result', 'The third one surprised even me').
formats.when: Longer (20–60 s) educational or reveal videos where you need to protect mid-video retention, and multi-part series.
steps: Promise a specific payoff in the hook, not a vague 'you won't believe'.
Show a blurred or partial glimpse of the end state.
Pay off late, but before the final 20% of the video, then loop or add a CTA.
Always pay off. Bait-and-switch drives swipe-aways and 'not interested' feedback.

example.creator: Genre-wide convention ('wait for it' / reveal-at-end)
example.description: The 'wait for it' caption and the delayed reveal are long-standing native short-form conventions. Serialised storytellers such as Reesa Teesa (see storytime) end each part on an unresolved beat.

formats.evidence: Mechanism: Instagram weighs absolute and relative watch time (Mosseri), and TikTok gives greater weight to watching a longer video to the end (TikTok Newsroom, 2020). Open loops target those signals. There is no direct study of 'curiosity gap' hooks, so this is practitioner evidence.

production.transitions: A progress cue (counter or timer) to keep the viewer oriented

formats.name: Shock Stat Opener
formats.definition: Open with one surprising, specific, sourced number as giant on-screen text and say it aloud.
formats.when: Biohacking, DEXA, ice-bath science and training. Numbers stop the scroll and make the post saveable and sendable. Only use real, citable numbers.
steps: Use one precise number ('11 minutes a week', '31% body fat at a BMI of 23'), not a range.
Make the number the largest element in frame 1.
Flash the source on screen and put it in the caption.
Translate the stat into one personal action.

example.creator: Andrew Huberman (Huberman Lab)
example.description: Popularised '~11 minutes per week' of total deliberate cold exposure, a figure drawn from Søberg et al. 2021 (Cell Reports Medicine) on winter swimmers.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Specific, concrete numbers are a staple of high-CTR headlines, but no platform study isolates them. Saves and sends are the relevant signals (Mosseri, Jan 2025; Metricool 2026 shows carousels lead on saves).

formats.name: Listicle ('3 things / 5 mistakes')
formats.definition: A numbered-beats structure where each item is one visual and one line.
formats.when: Educational, save-driven content. Use 3–5 items in a Reel to keep the pace and 5–10 in a carousel.
steps: Put the count in the hook ('3 signs your back pain is muscular').
Give each item a visual change and an on-screen number.
Save the strongest item for last, or tease it ('number 3 is the one nobody does').
End with 'save this for your next session'.

example.creator: Genre-wide educational format
example.description: Numbered tip videos and carousels are standard across fitness, health and photography education accounts.

formats.evidence: Carousel data supports list structures. Socialinsider's 2020 study (about 22M posts) found 10-slide carousels had the highest average engagement (over 2%). Metricool's June 2026 study (24.3M posts) found carousels lead on saves.

production.transitions: A cut per item, with a number overlay
production.audio: Voice or trending audio with text

formats.name: Storytime / Serialised Story
formats.definition: A narrative told to camera (often while doing something else) with a cliffhanger structure, sometimes split into numbered parts.
formats.when: Client stories (anonymised), founder stories, 'the client who…' case studies. It builds parasocial trust and drives follows for the next part.
steps: Lead with the most dramatic line of the story, not the beginning.
Keep visual movement going (walking, prepping the room, filling the plunge) so the frame isn't static.
End each part on an open question and label it 'Part 1/3'.
Pin the next part, or link the series in comments.

example.creator: Reesa Teesa (@reesamteesa)
example.description: 'Who TF Did I Marry?!' (February 2024), a roughly 50-part talking-head storytime series about her ex-husband that became a TikTok phenomenon.
example.stats: Widely reported at ~400M cumulative views (Feb–Mar 2024; not re-verified this session)

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Mosseri says likes per reach matter more for connected (follower) distribution, and series turn viewers into followers. Watch-time mechanics (relative and absolute) reward stories that hold.

formats.name: 'Day X of…' Series / Challenge
formats.definition: A recurring numbered series documenting progress ('Day 14 of daily ice baths', 'Week 6 of my DEXA recomposition').
formats.when: Building habitual return viewers and a follower base. It suits gyms (client recomposition), ice bath (streaks) and biohacking (protocols with measurable checkpoints).
steps: Put 'Day X' in frame-1 text and keep the same framing every day for continuity.
Show one metric each episode (temperature, minutes, body-fat %, HRV).
Mark milestones (day 1, 7, 30) with a bigger reveal.
Batch-film to keep the series consistent.

example.creator: #75Hard participants (program created by Andy Frisella)
example.description: Thousands of creators document 'Day X of 75 Hard' as a daily progress series.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Series strengthen connected-audience signals (likes per reach weigh more for followers, per Mosseri, Jan 2025). Trial Reels let you test series episodes on non-followers without fatiguing followers. No direct study found.

production.audio: Natural sound plus a short VO

formats.name: Before / After Reveal & Transformation
formats.definition: Contrast a 'before' state with an 'after' state through a hard cut, a wipe or a split. Examples: raw vs graded photo, posture or range of motion before and after a session, body recomposition with DEXA numbers.
formats.when: Proof-of-result content for every niche. Caution: Meta's ad policies restrict before/after body images in health and weight-loss ads, so treat this as an organic-only format for body content. Get explicit client consent and avoid medical claims (especially massage).
steps: Match the framing, lighting and angle between before and after so the change reads instantly.
Show 'after' for a split second first (outcome-first), then 'before' leading into the transformation.
Use objective numbers where possible (DEXA %, range-of-motion degrees, a time).
Put a timeframe and a disclaimer in the caption.

example.creator: Dr. Pimple Popper (Dr. Sandra Lee)
example.description: A dermatologist whose before/after procedure videos (with satisfying, sensory footage) built a massive YouTube/TikTok audience and a TV show.

formats.evidence: OpusClip 2026: showing the product or outcome early is the top hook category. Visual contrast is processed fast, which fits a 1–3 s decision window. No direct before/after study found.

production.transitions: A hard cut, swipe/wipe, or slider split; speed ramp only for photo/video showreels
production.audio: A beat drop on the reveal, or VO

formats.name: Myth-Bust
formats.definition: Name a popular belief, label it myth or fact, and show the evidence ('Myth: ice baths burn fat').
formats.when: Positioning as a trusted expert. It pairs well with green-screen evidence and works as a carousel ('5 massage myths').
steps: Show 'MYTH:' plus the belief in frame 1.
Give your verdict within 3 s (true, false, or 'it depends').
Show one piece of evidence (a study, a demo, your data).
Close with the practical rule.

example.creator: Jeff Nippard
example.description: Science-based fitness creator known for evidence-reviewed myth-busting on training and nutrition.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. OpusClip 2026 lists 'Expert Explainer' as among the most common viral storylines. Myth-busts are save- and send-worthy, the signals Mosseri named.

formats.name: Test / Experiment
formats.definition: Run a mini-experiment on camera and report the result ('I did 3-minute ice baths daily for 30 days and tracked my HRV', 'Phone vs €5,000 camera: can you tell?').
formats.when: Biohacking and DEXA studios (measurable outcomes), photographers (gear or lighting tests), gyms (protocol comparisons). It needs an honest result even when it's boring.
steps: State the hypothesis and the measurement in the hook.
Show the method fast (setup, 1–2 s per step).
Reveal the result with a number or a side-by-side.
Add the caveat (n=1) and invite viewers to suggest the next test.

example.creator: Mark Rober
example.description: Former NASA engineer whose experiment-driven builds and tests ('I built X to test Y') are among YouTube's most-watched science content.

formats.evidence: OpusClip's 'Comparative Showdown' hook category (A vs B) was among its top performers, which the vendor says average 3–5x more views than the weakest categories. This is vendor data.

production.transitions: A split-screen for A vs B; a timer overlay

formats.name: Comparison Showdown (X vs Y / Cheap vs Expensive)
formats.definition: Two options compared head to head, often at extreme price or quality points ('€20 massage vs €200 massage', 'Phone vs cinema camera', 'Bathtub vs dedicated plunge').
formats.when: Justifying premium pricing, explaining a service difference, gear content for photographers.
steps: Put both options on screen in frame 1 (a split or quick alternation).
Compare 3 attributes, one beat each.
Give a clear verdict ('who should pick which').
Avoid disparaging named competitors.

example.creator: MrBeast
example.description: Price-ladder comparison videos such as '$1 vs $1,000,000 Hotel Room!' on YouTube.

formats.evidence: OpusClip 2026 names 'Comparative Showdown' among the top hook categories (3–5x the views of weaker categories, vendor data).

formats.name: Comment-Reply Video
formats.definition: A video answering a specific viewer comment, with the comment shown as an on-screen sticker (TikTok's 'Reply to comment with video'; Instagram supports replying to comments with a Reel).
formats.when: Turning FAQs and objections ('Is a DEXA scan safe?', 'Does deep tissue have to hurt?') into content. It signals community responsiveness and gives you endless topics.
steps: Pick comments with a question or objection, not just praise.
Show the comment sticker in frame 1 and answer in the first sentence.
Demonstrate the answer rather than only telling it.
Tag or notify the commenter so they come back and engage.

example.creator: Genre-wide native feature
example.description: TikTok's comment-reply sticker labels the video 'Replying to @username'. Educators and brands use it to answer FAQs at scale.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. No public study on comment-reply performance was found. Mechanism: it answers real search-like intent, which matters given that roughly half of US consumers have used TikTok as a search engine (Adobe Express survey, 2026).

formats.name: ASMR / Sensory
formats.definition: Content built around close, crisp natural sound and texture: oil on skin, hands working a muscle, ice cracking, water entering a plunge, breath, shutter clicks, the beep of a DEXA arm moving.
formats.when: Massage and ice bath above all, plus photographers (gear and shutter sounds). It works as a relaxing or satisfying format and is less dependent on language, which suits multilingual Swiss audiences.
steps: Record close to the source with a lav or shotgun mic. Phone mics pick up room hiss.
Use tight macro framing and slow, deliberate motion.
Use no music, or very low ambient music under the natural sound.
Use minimal text (one line) so viewers can watch without reading.
Get written client consent for any body footage.

example.creator: Dr. Beau Hightower (chiropractor)
example.description: A chiropractor whose adjustment videos, built around the sensory 'crack' and the patient's reaction, drew very large TikTok and YouTube audiences.

formats.evidence: Sound matters on these platforms. 88% of TikTok users say sound is essential to the experience (TikTok/Kantar, 2021), and over 80% of Instagram Reels are played with sound on (Meta, cited via Meta/Toluna study coverage). No ASMR-specific platform study was found.

production.audio: Natural sound first, optionally with low ambient music

formats.name: Satisfying Process
formats.definition: A complete, smooth process shown start to finish with a clear end state: setting up a treatment table, a plunge filling and icing over, a photo edit from raw to final, a DEXA scan pass.
formats.when: Low-talk, high-rewatch content and loopable B-roll for any service with a tactile or visual process.
steps: Lock off the camera (tripod) for stable, clean motion.
Show the finish briefly in frame 1, or promise it in text.
Speed-ramp slow parts and keep the satisfying moment at real speed.
End where the loop restarts cleanly.

example.creator: Genre-wide (#oddlysatisfying, #pressurewashing)
example.description: Pressure-washing, cleaning and restoration process videos are a long-running 'satisfying' genre on TikTok and Reels.

formats.evidence: Mechanism: completion and rewatch. TikTok weights finishing a video (TikTok Newsroom, 2020), and Instagram ranks on watch time (Mosseri, Jan 2025). Practitioner evidence; no isolated study.

production.transitions: Speed ramps on the boring parts; a seamless loop point

formats.name: Split-Screen
formats.definition: Two video panels at once: talking head plus demo, before plus after, A plus B, or (infamously) a talking clip over unrelated gameplay ('sludge content').
formats.when: Use your own footage on both halves (talking head plus your B-roll, or a technique comparison). Don't use unrelated third-party filler footage: Instagram's 2024 and 2026 originality rules demote reposted and aggregated material.
steps: Use a top/bottom split for 9:16, with faces in the top half and the demo in the bottom.
Keep both halves relevant to the same idea.
Keep captions in the central band, out of the bottom UI zone.
Only use a split when both halves add information.

example.creator: Genre-wide ('sludge content')
example.description: Talking clips stacked over Subway Surfers or Minecraft gameplay, widely covered as a retention hack in 2022–2023. Cited here as an anti-pattern under current originality rules.

formats.evidence: No study shows split-screen helps by itself. Originality enforcement (Instagram, April 2024 and April 2026) is the main constraint.

formats.name: Text-Wall / 'Read the Caption' Bait
formats.definition: A short looping clip with a paragraph of on-screen text (or 'read the caption ↓') so the viewer stays or rewatches while reading.
formats.when: Hot takes, client stories or lists when you can't film new footage. Use sparingly, because it can feel low-effort, and on Instagram the visual should still be your own original footage.
steps: Loop 5–8 s of your own aesthetic B-roll (the studio, the plunge, gear).
Use 2–4 lines of text, large and high-contrast, inside the safe zone.
Make the first line a hook and finish the story in the caption.
Use music at low volume, or natural sound.

example.creator: Genre-wide
example.description: Common among meme, quote and educator accounts. The B-roll loops while viewers read, which inflates watch time per view.

formats.evidence: Mechanism: Instagram counts both absolute and relative watch time (Mosseri), so reading time counts and short loops replay. No study confirms a reach lift, and aggregator-style text posts made from others' footage now lose recommendation eligibility (April 2026).

formats.name: Seamless Loop Ending
formats.definition: The last frame or last line flows straight back into the first, so viewers rewatch before they notice the restart.
formats.when: Short (under 15 s) visual pieces: plunge entry, a photo reveal, a massage stroke sequence, a text-wall loop.
steps: Plan the last shot to match the first in framing and motion direction.
For speech, end mid-sentence on a word that completes the opening line.
Avoid an end card or logo outro, which breaks the loop.
Keep it short, because loops work best under about 15 s.

example.creator: Genre-wide editing technique
example.description: Seamless-loop edits and sentence loops are common short-form retention techniques.

formats.evidence: TikTok weights completion of longer videos (Newsroom, 2020). Instagram ranks on watch time (Mosseri, Jan 2025). YouTube has counted every replay as a Shorts view since 31 March 2025 ('engaged views' are tracked separately). Practitioner evidence otherwise.

production.transitions: A match cut from last to first frame
production.audio: A music loop that resolves on beat

formats.name: Trending Audio / Lip-Sync / Skit
formats.definition: A video built on a trending sound or a lip-synced dialogue clip, or a short comedic skit using the platform's sound library.
formats.when: Personality and brand vibe, relatable humour, reach bursts. For business accounts, check the music is in the commercial library, and don't let a trend replace your niche signal.
steps: Pick a sound early in its curve (rising in the audio browser or Creative Center).
Map the sound's beats to your niche situation (therapist vs client, coach vs member).
Keep it to one joke and one setup, landing before the drop.
Add a niche-specific text overlay so the content is still topically classifiable.

example.creator: Nathan Apodaca (@420doggface208); Sabrina Bahsoon ('Tube Girl')
example.description: Apodaca's September 2020 skateboard clip to Fleetwood Mac's 'Dreams' sent the 1977 song back onto the charts. Bahsoon's August 2023 lip-syncs on the London Underground (wide-angle, low phone angle) became a widely copied trend.
example.stats: 'Dreams' re-entered the Billboard Hot 100 in Oct 2020 after the clip (widely reported)

formats.evidence: Instagram Ranking Explained (2023): one of the key Reels predictions is how likely you are to go to the audio page. TikTok (2020): sounds are part of the 'video information' used for recommendations. Carousels with music became eligible for the Reels tab in October 2024. Business accounts have restricted music libraries (verify in-app).

formats.name: Talking Head + B-roll
formats.definition: The expert speaks to camera, with B-roll cutaways illustrating each claim and bold captions throughout.
formats.when: The workhorse for authority and education in every niche. The face builds trust, the B-roll keeps visual change, and the captions cover muted viewing.
steps: Script a 1-sentence hook, 3 beats and a 1-line close. Cut every pause.
Cut to B-roll on each noun ('hip flexors' shows the hip flexor stretch).
Use animated, high-contrast captions in the center safe zone.
Film A-roll at eye level with soft window light and a clip-on mic.

example.creator: Alex Hormozi
example.description: Short-form business clips that combine a talking head, fast cuts, B-roll and bold, animated word-by-word captions. The style is widely copied ('Hormozi captions').

formats.evidence: OpusClip 2026: 80.2% of viral-tier clips used captions and 78.6% used animated captions. 'Expert Explainer' was among the most common storylines. Meta (secondhand): sponsored Reels with a human presence had about 27% higher CTR.

production.transitions: Hard cuts and punch-in zooms; no flashy transitions
production.audio: Voice plus a low music bed

formats.name: Hands-Only + Voiceover
formats.definition: An overhead or close shot of hands performing the technique, with a voiceover or text. No face.
formats.when: Massage technique demos (protects client privacy), photo editing or retouching, gear setups, ice-bath prep. Good for camera-shy owners and multilingual VO versions (DE/FR/EN).
steps: Shoot from directly overhead or over the shoulder on a tripod.
Use clean surfaces and good light. Hands and texture are the hero.
Write the VO after the edit, timed to the visible actions.
Export language variants with the same visuals.

example.creator: BuzzFeed Tasty
example.description: Overhead, hands-only recipe videos that became one of the defining social-video formats of the mid-2010s.

formats.evidence: Booyah, citing Brand Lift research: Reels ads with music plus voiceover scored 15 points higher on positive response than those without sound. That is ad data, reported secondhand.

production.audio: VO plus low music, or natural sound

formats.name: Behind the Scenes (BTS)
formats.definition: Show the work behind the result: shoot setups, studio opening routines, how a DEXA scan works, ice delivery, prep for a client.
formats.when: Building trust and demystifying a service before a first booking. For photographers, BTS is the core growth format.
steps: Open with the final result or the most surprising part of the setup.
Show 3–6 quick process shots with labels.
Include a human moment (a mistake, a laugh, a client reaction).
End on the result again.

example.creator: Peter McKinnon
example.description: A photographer and filmmaker whose behind-the-scenes and B-roll technique videos built one of the largest photo/video audiences on YouTube and Instagram.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. Fits Mosseri's Dec 2025 view that authenticity signals matter more as AI makes polish cheap. That is commentary, not a stated ranking boost.

production.transitions: Hard cuts; optional speed ramps for setup

formats.name: Price / Value Reveal
formats.definition: Reveal what something costs or what you get for a price ('What CHF 150 gets you at a Zürich DEXA studio').
formats.when: Removing price anxiety before booking, premium positioning, comparing value. Swiss audiences are price-sensitive, so transparency builds trust.
steps: Put the price in frame-1 text.
Walk through everything included, one beat per item.
Show the client experience, not just the room.
Close with who it's for.

example.creator: Salary Transparent Street (Hannah Williams)
example.description: Street interviews asking 'How much money do you make?' that grew rapidly in 2022 and turned pay transparency into a format.

formats.evidence: Practitioner evidence. It answers search-like intent: roughly half of US consumers have used TikTok as a search engine (Adobe Express survey, 2026).

production.audio: VO or trending sound with text

formats.name: Authority / Expert Explainer
formats.definition: Lead with the credential ('Physio of 12 years here', 'As a DEXA technician…'), then explain one thing clearly.
formats.when: Health-adjacent niches where trust gates booking (DEXA, massage therapy, cold exposure). Combine it with myth-bust, green-screen or comment-reply.
steps: Give the credential in 3 words, then the claim, inside 3 s.
Use one concept per video, with a diagram, prop or demo.
Use plain language and no jargon without a translation.
Cite sources in the caption.

example.creator: Dr. Karan Rajan (@drkaranrajan)
example.description: A UK NHS surgeon whose quick, credentialed health explainers built a very large TikTok following.

formats.evidence: OpusClip 2026: 'Expert Explainer' was among the most common viral storylines (14,213-clip storyline subset; vendor data).

formats.name: Trial Reels (Instagram test-to-non-followers)
formats.definition: An Instagram feature: a Reel published as a 'trial' is shown only to non-followers first. You see its performance, then choose whether to share it to followers.
formats.when: Testing risky hooks, new formats, A/B versions of the same video (different first 3 s), or off-brand experiments without fatiguing or confusing existing followers.
steps: Toggle 'Trial' when posting a Reel (public professional accounts; eligibility has expanded since launch).
Post 2–3 hook variants of the same body as separate trials.
Compare trials only against other trials (Mosseri), using sends, likes and watch time.
Share the winner to followers. Instagram later added an option to auto-share a trial that performs well (reported; verify in-app).

example.creator: Instagram / Adam Mosseri (feature launch)
example.description: Launched December 2024 and later expanded to more creators. Mosseri warned that trials will 'almost always' get less reach than normal Reels because they don't go to followers.

formats.evidence: Official feature (Instagram). Mosseri's guidance: compare trials to trials and look at sends, likes and watch time. Third-party claims of reach multipliers for trials are unverified.

production.transitions: Same body; vary only the first 3 s

formats.name: Borrowed Formula (proven idea, your twist)
formats.definition: Take an idea that already went viral for someone else, keep its skeleton (hook, structure, payoff) and remake it with your own brand, client or niche as the twist. The structure is what earns the views, so it keeps working whoever repeats it.
formats.when: Every week, as the safe bet next to new ideas. Works best while the original is still circulating and when your twist is obvious in the first 2 seconds. Borrow the idea; shoot your own footage and write your own words.
steps: Pick one proven post: Hall of Fame or Favourites in this hub, or anything far above its niche's usual numbers.
Write down its skeleton: the first line or frame, the structure in beats, and the payoff.
Choose one twist that makes it yours: your client, your studio, your product, your niche.
Shoot it with your own footage and words, keeping the original's timing.
Post it while the idea is still circulating, then compare its 3-second hold with your usual posts.

example.creator: PostProtocol (@thepostprotocol)
example.description: A breakdown reel Constantin saved: it shows one account's idea being borrowed by another brand with its own twist, and the formula working again. The cover shows the first video at 43.5M.
example.stats: 1,640 likes · 547 comments on the breakdown reel (Instagram embed page, 2026-11-09)

formats.evidence: In this hub: the same LOVE trend (letters spelled around the body, the O made with the arms) worked for three different gym accounts in All-time favourites: @shubham_fitnesx 90,467 likes, @tiboinshape 55,816 likes and @stayclassycrossfit 6,176 likes, each read from the post's Instagram embed page.
